# In vivo multi‑parameter mapping of the habenula using MRI

Giorgia Milotta 1*, Isobel Green 2, Jonathan P. Roiser 3 & Martina F. Callaghan 1

The habenula is a small, epithalamic brain structure situated between the mediodorsal thalamus and the third ventricle. It plays an important role in the reward circuitry of the brain and is implicated in psychiatric conditions, such as depression. The importance of the habenula for human cognition and mental health make it a key structure of interest for neuroimaging studies. However, few studies have characterised the physical properties of the human habenula using magnetic resonance imaging because its challenging visualisation in vivo, primarily due to its subcortical location and small size. To date, microstructural characterization of the habenula has focused on quantitative susceptibility mapping. In this work, we complement this previous characterisation with measures of longitudinal and effective transverse relaxation rates, proton density and magnetisation transfer saturation using a high-resolution quantitative multi-parametric mapping protocol at 3T, in a cohort of 26 healthy participants. The habenula had consistent boundaries across the various parameter maps and was most clearly visualised on the longitudinal relaxation rate maps. We have provided a quantitative multi-parametric characterisation that may be useful for future sequence optimisation to enhance visualisation of the habenula, and additionally provides reference values for future studies investigating pathological differences in habenula microstructure.

The habenula is a small, epithalamic brain structure situated between the mediodorsal thalamus and the third ventricle, rostral to the posterior ­commissure1,2. It is thought to be involved in basic neural mechanisms that are key to survival, in particular aversive ­processing3. It receives inputs from the limbic forebrain via the stria medullaris, and sends efferents to the midbrain via the fasciculus retroflexus, forming a transmission system from forebrain to monoaminergic midbrain known as the dorsal diencephalic conduction ­system4. Given this connectivity, the habenula is uniquely poised to convey—and mediate—the flow of information from the limbic forebrain to key midbrain regions involved in regulating mood and emotional behaviours. It has long been known to be centrally involved in processes such as sleep, aversion, pain, sexual and maternal behaviours, and anxiety. Lesions to and stimulation of the habenula have been shown to alter behaviour in each of these ­domains5. Interest in the habenula has intensified in recent years due to findings that the lateral habenula (LHb) influences dopaminergic processing of valenced stimuli, i.e. rewards and punishments, and cues indicating their ­delivery6. Dopaminergic neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and substantia nigra (SN), to which the LHb sends disynaptic inputs, are responsive to rewards and punishments, activating robustly to both rewards and reward-predictive cues, and showing altered activity in response to aversive stimuli and ­cues7. Direct stimulation of the LHb has been shown to profoundly inhibit activation in midbrain dopamine ­neurons8,9, and lesions of the habenula reduce inhibition in the dopaminergic midbrain following reward omission (see Tian and ­Uchida10). The privileged position the LHb plays in regulating dopamine neuron function has prompted investigation of its role in depression given that several core symptoms, such as anhedonia and disrupted decision-making, have been linked to dopamine ­dysfunction11. The handful of human neuroimaging studies examining habenula activation have verified that it is activated upon delivery of cues predicting aversive outcomes, and inhibited in response to cues predicting ­reward12; and compelling studies of habenula activation in individuals with depression have repeatedly shown altered ­activation13–17. However, the direction and context specificity of these changes remains to be clarified, and future human neuroimaging studies will be essential to clarify the precise nature of altered habenula function in conditions such as depression. The importance of the habenula for human cognition and mental health thus make it a key structure of interest for neuroimaging studies. However, relatively few studies have been conducted in humans because habenula visualisation in vivo is challenging, primarily due to its subcortical location and small ­size18–21 in the range of 15–30 ­mm3. Anatomical visualization of the habenula, and robust definition of its boundaries, is contingent on having sufficient image contrast between the habenula and its surroundings. Imaging of the habenula has primarily exploited its high density of myelinated ­fibres18,19, which reduce the longitudinal relaxation time ­(T1) enhancing its visualization on ­T1-weighted ­images18. For this reason, ­T1-weighted images have most commonly been used to manually segment the ­habenula18,19. Schenck et al.25 observed increased magnetic susceptibility in the habenula, suggesting an iron-rich sub-structure26 as observed for several other sub-cortical brain ­regions27,28. Increased iron content also serves to shorten ­T1 ­times29. Quantitative susceptibility mapping (QSM) has shown promising results in characterizing the origin of contrast, facilitating habenula ­visualization24,25. Nevertheless, habenula delineation and characterization remains challenging due to its small size, which makes it vulnerable to partial volume effects. This motivates a push towards higher (sub-mm) resolution to improve the precision with which the habenula can be delineated. Yoo et al.23 combined high-resolution (< 0.8 mm isotropic) imaging of the habenula with QSM to investigate its sub-structure and provided reference QSM values for future in vivo studies. They found an anterior–posterior gradient in susceptibility values that correlated with visual conspicuity scores. However, this pattern was inconsistent across individuals. To date, microstructural characterization of the habenula has focused on QSM to disentangle paramagnetic iron and diamagnetic myelin contributions. In this work we complement this characterization with measures of the longitudinal and effective transverse relaxation rates ­[R1 (= 1/T1) and ­R2* respectively], proton density (PD) and magnetisation transfer saturation (MTsat) using a high-resolution (0.8 mm isotropic) quantitative multi-parametric mapping (MPM) protocol at 3T, in a cohort of 26 healthy participants. These physical properties are sensitive to key biological features such as myelin, iron and water content, and may therefore inform improvements in habenula visualisation and our understanding of its ­microstructure30,31. For each participant, the habenula was manually delineated, its volume computed and the MPM values extracted from this region of interest (ROI). To investigate which metric was best suited to delineating the habenula we also computed the contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) between the habenula and the surrounding grey matter (GM) tissue. We further investigated the degree of alignment that could be achieved after spatial normalisation to a group template (Montreal Neurological Institute, MNI), which has previously been reported to be ­poor19.

Results Native space characterisation. R1, ­R2*, PD and MTsat maps were computed for each of the 26 study participants using the hMRI ­toolbox32. MTsat maps from two participants were discarded due to artefacts present in the MT-weighted images. Example maps from one representative participant are shown in Fig. 1 along with zoomed views focusing on the habenula. For a better habenula depiction, Supporting Information Fig. S1 shows the habenula ROI overlaid on the ­R1 map for another representative participant. The habenula ROI was manually defined according to the geometric protocol described in Lawson et al19. The mean (± standard deviation) of each parameter, across participants, within this habenula ROI was ­R1 = 0.86 ± 0.03 1/s, ­R2* = 19.11 ± 1.87 1/s, PD = 76.21 ± 1.52% and MTsat = 1.05 ± 0.08% (Fig. 2). The left and right habenula volumes and the averaged left and right habenula volume for each participant are shown in Fig. 3. The mean (± standard deviation), across participants, of the averaged volume was 19.26 ± 2.03 ­mm3 with similar left (19.57 ± 2.56 ­mm3) and right (18.94 ± 2.30 ­mm3) habenula volumes. Finally, the mean ± standard deviation of the habenula volume normalised to that of the entire brain, across the cohort, was 8.3 × ­10−3 ± 1.3 × ­10−3%. The contrast to noise ratio (CNR) was computed between the habenula and the surrounding grey matter (GM) and is shown in Fig. 4. The ­R1 maps had the highest CNR with a mean (± standard deviation) across participants of 1.34 ± 0.03. The ­R2* and MTsat maps also had positive CNR (i.e. hyperintense habenula relative to the surrounding GM) with mean values across participants of 0.70 ± 0.03 and 0.57 ± 0.33 respectively. On the PD maps, the habenula was hypointense relative to the surrounding GM leading to a negative CNR of − 0.67 ± 0.22.

Group space CNR. Spatial normalisation using the Dartel ­algorithm33 was used to align the quantitative maps to normalized space. The cohort-average maps are shown in Fig. 5 along with a zoomed view focusing on the habenula (arrows). Figure 6 indicates the probability, for this cohort, that a voxel lies within the habenula, superimposed on the cohort-average ­R1 map. The maximum probability was 0.77. This amounts to a voxel being consistently defined as being within the habenula for 22 of the 26 participants, but only occurred for two voxels. No voxels were consistently found to be within the habenula for every participant in the cohort. CNR was also computed on the cohort-average maps in normalized space (Fig. 7). In keeping with the CNR computed per participant, the ­R1 maps had highest CNR. As the definition of the habenula became more conservative (higher probability of being within the habenula) the CNR increased.

Discussion The habenula has attracted much interest in neuroscience studies because it plays an important role in the reward circuitry of the brain and is implicated in psychiatric conditions, such as ­depression9,10,17. However, imaging the habenula remains challenging due to its sub-cortical location and small size, with few reports analysing its microstructural composition in vivo23–25. To address this gap in the literature, we performed a multi-parametric characterisation of the microstructure of the habenula by quantifying relaxation rates ­(R1, ­R2*), water content (PD) and a marker of macromolecular

This suggests that, among the four quantitative maps considered in this analysis, the ­R1 map is the most suitable choice for segmenting the habenula. In prior habenula research T1-weighted images have been most commonly used for this purpose. ­R1 maps mirror the contrast in T1-weighted images, but additionally offer the advantage of not being confounded by hardware-driven contrast (e.g. due to spatial variation in transmit and receive fields) and of having less vulnerability to other sequence settings (e.g. the echo time dictates the degree of additional ­T2* weighting in a ­T1-weighted image but is corrected for in an ­R1 map). Therefore, ­R1 maps might also be preferable for more reliable habenula segmentation with respect to T1-weighted images. The habenula was segmented on ­R1 maps, whereas the segmentation procedure described ­in19 (which was followed for the delineation of the ROIs) was performed on ­T1-weighted images. In this work, a lower mean volume across the left and right habenulae was observed in comparison to reports in the literature using ­MRI19,23 or post mortem ­histology20. When a stricter definition of the habenula is adopted (threshold > 0.3) voxels with partial volume between the habenula and surrounding GM or CSF are excluded from the analysis and thus an increase in CNR is observed. The noise reduction obtained due to averaging following spatial normalization further improves the CNR. Consistent with native space findings, the highest CNR is obtained on the normalized ­R1 maps. One of the main limitations of the proposed work is that the habenula ROIs were defined by a single individual (IG), and no reliability analysis was performed. However, the delineation of the habenulae followed a well-defined ­procedure19 and the capacity to visualise the habenula was bolstered by the use of an ­R1 map with high spatial resolution. The cohort size was also modest. However, as noted previously, the consistency of the measurements bodes well for future optimisation of habenula visualisation. However, a larger cohort would be needed to confirm this consistency in microstructure or to assess any meaningful inter-individual ­variation39. CNR was only measured between habenula and GM. The contrast between the habenula and ventricular CSF was not considered in the analysis. This approach was adopted because the contrast between the CSF and habenula is usually sufficiently high to aid its visualization, whereas delineation with respect to GM is usually more challenging. However, the contrast with respect to CSF is particularly high on the MTsat map, but this was not captured in the CNR analysis due to its focus on GM. With suitable computation of the signal phase, the MPM protocol could naturally be augmented to include QSM without any extension of the acquisition time. Given that QSM has shown promise in depicting the habenula, suggesting the presence of iron-rich substructure, this would provide a more complete characterisation of habenula microstructure.

Conclusion We have provided a quantitative multi-parametric characterization of the habenula microstructure in vivo in a sample of 26 healthy participants. The results suggest that the habenula can be most clearly visualised on longitudinal relaxation rate ­(R1) maps. This characterisation provides baseline measurements that may be useful for sequence optimization to further enhance visualisation, and provide reference values for future studies investigating pathological differences in habenula microstructure.

Methods Data acquisition. MPM protocol.  Data were acquired on a Siemens 3T Prisma using a 64-channel head and neck receiver coil. A Multi-Parameter Mapping (MPM) protocol, as described by Callaghan et al.40, was used for image acquisition. In brief, it comprised three RF- and gradient-spoiled multi-echo 3D FLASH scans acquired with ­T1 (αT1w = 21°), PD (αPDw = 6°) or MT (αMTw = 6°) weighting. To achieve MT-weighting a 4 ms Gaussian RF pulse at 2 kHz off-resonance with flip angle of 220˚ was applied prior to excitation. The ratio of these low-resolution (8 ­mm3 isotropic resolution) images was used to estimate the position-specific net receiver sensitivity of the array coil, which was then used to correct for movement between the ­acquisitions43.

Imaging sessions.  Data were acquired on 26 participants (12 males). The participants were recruited for a functional MRI study. Participants ranged in age from 20 to 43, mean age was 24.36 (standard deviation 4.88), all participant were right handed. All data acquisition was approved by the Central London Research Ethics Committee 3, and all methods were performed in accordance with specified regulations. All participants gave written informed consent for the study prior to data acquisition.

Data analysis. All images were analysed using ­SPM1244 (Wellcome Centre for Human Neuroimaging, London, UK). ­R1, ­R2*, PD and MTsat maps were generated for each participant using the hMRI ­toolbox32. The habenula delineation was performed on the ­R1 maps because of its optimal depiction of the habenula. The definition procedure was performed following the geometric approach described by Lawson et al.19. ­R1 maps of each participant were rotated and translated until the midpoint of the posterior commissure was aligned with the midpoint of the anterior commissure. On the re-oriented ­R1 maps, the left and right habenulae regions of interest (ROIs) were manually drawn on the re-oriented ­R1 maps. An inverse transformation, including rotation and translation, was then applied to the ROI masks to re-orient them back to the native space of the ­R1 maps.

Spatial normalization of the ­R1, ­R2*, PD, MTsat, GM probability maps and binarised habenulae ROI was performed using the Dartel toolbox in SPM. This procedure included the following steps:

1.	 Generation of GM and white matter (WM) tissues classes via segmentation of the T1-weighted image for each participant. 2. The CNR between the habenula and surrounding GM defined in normalized space was calculated on the cohort-averaged ­R1, ­R2*, PD and MTsat maps in normalized space. The CNR was measured while varying the probability map threshold defining the habenula. As the probability of being within the habenulae increased, the number of voxels within the habenulae ROI decreased, excluding more voxels that may contain partial volume of the surrounding GM from the analysis. The GM ROI was kept constant and defined by the logical intersection between the average whole-brain GM mask in normalized space and the outer habenula mask. # Shifting attention to orient or avoid: a unifying account of the tail of the striatum and its dopaminergic inputs

**Authors:** Isobel Green; Ryunosuke Amo; Mitsuko Watabe-Uchida

**Affiliations:** Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology, Center for Brain Science, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA

## Abstract

The tail of the striatum (TS) is increasingly recognized as a unique subdivision of the striatum, characterized by its dense sensory inputs and projections received from a distinct group of dopamine neurons. Separate lines of research have characterized the functional role of TS, and TS-projecting dopamine neurons, in three realms: saccadic eye movement towards valuable visual stimuli; tone-guided choice between two options; and defensive responses to threatening stimuli. We propose a framework for reconciling these diverse roles as varied implementations of a conserved response to salient stimuli, with dopamine in TS providing a teaching signal to promote quick attentional shifts that facilitate stimulus-driven orientation and/or avoidance.

## Introduction

Historically, the striatum has been classified into several divisions based on connectivity and function [1]. Recent studies in rodents have started to re-appreciate one of these divisions, the ‘tail of the striatum’ (TS), named for its anatomical homology to the caudate tail (CDt) in primates [2–7]. Here, we first review the anatomy of TS and its connectivity, then discuss evidence implicating TS and TS-projecting dopamine neurons in diverse behavioral functions. Finally, we suggest that these apparently disparate accounts of TS function can be understood in a common framework, in which TS identifies physically salient stimuli and directs a rapid attentional shift to promote stimulus-responsive behavior necessary for survival.

## Anatomical features of TS

Anatomically, TS is considered to be the sensory domain of the striatum. TS receives dense projections from visual and auditory cortices and thalamus, but unlike adjacent dorsolateral striatum (DLS), receives few projections from somatosensory and motor cortices [3,4,8–11] (Figure 1B). Unlike the dorsomedial striatum (DMS), TS receives few projections from the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), yet receives strong projections from the temporal association cortex (TeA), a multi-modal object recognition area. This suggests segregation of information flow between anterior and posterior caudate (DMS and TS, respectively). TS receives projections from a unique group of dopamine neurons spanning the caudolateral substantia nigra pars compacta (clSNc) and the substantia nigra pars lateralis (SNL) (Figure 1A). These dopamine neurons in turn receive inputs distinct from dopamine neurons projecting to the rest of the striatum, including the zona incerta (ZI) and the intermediate layer of the superior colliculus (SC), the multi-modal integration center for orienting and avoidance [5,12].

Like other striatal subregions, TS is mainly composed of two types of projection neurons: D1 receptor-expressing medium spiny neurons (D1-MSNs) and D2-MSNs [13–15]. D1-MSNs primarily target the caudo-dorsolateral substantia nigra reticulata (cdlSNr) and SNL, (‘direct pathway’); D2-MSNs target the caudoventral globus pallidus (cvGP or cvGPe) which in turn targets cdlSNr/SNL (‘indirect pathway’) [13,16]. The cvGP also targets other regions including the caudal thalamic reticular nucleus (cTRN), a visual and auditory processing center [17]. The cdlSNr/SNL sends dense projections to superior colliculus (SC) and inferior colliculus (IC), as well as periaqueductal gray (PAG) and cuneiform nucleus (CnF) [18,19]. Interconnected with various perceptual and sensorimotor brain areas, TS is well-positioned to link perception and action.

## Role of the CDt in Directed Eye Movements

TS is considered a homologue of CDt in primates, as both regions receive strong projections from auditory, visual and object cortices and thalamus, and few projections from prefrontal areas [3,4,8]. Consistent with its dense visual connectivity, stimulus-directed saccades robustly engage CDt and adjacent caudoventral putamen (putamen tail; PUTt). Electrophysiological recordings in macaques performing saccades to visual objects on a screen (Figure 2A) showed that CDt/PUTt neurons exhibit sharp stimulus selectivity and relatively large spatial selectivity [2,20,21], similar to visual responses in higher sensory cortical areas [20]. Notably, CDt neurons increased their activity to a stimulus in their visual and spatial receptive field both when stimuli were presented in the periphery as animals maintained center-screen fixation (passive viewing), and immediately before a saccade when animals were permitted to saccade (free viewing). The response to visual stimuli during fixation suggests that responses in CDt are stimulus-associated and not necessarily motor-evoked [21]. Further supporting CDt’s role in stimulus-directed saccades, electrical stimulation of CDt or optogenetic activation of CDt terminals in cdlSNr induced contralateral saccades during free viewing [16,21]. Furthermore, after saccades to certain stimuli were consistently rewarded, CDt/PUTt neurons responded more to the reward-predicting stimuli, paralleling the monkey’s gaze bias [22,23].

Similar to CDt, putative CDt-projecting dopamine neurons in the clSNc, unlike many other dopamine neurons, responded to reward-associated stimuli in the contralateral hemifield, but they did not consistently respond to reward itself [24]. Reward-associated stimulus responses were resistant to extinction, leading to the hypothesis that CDt neurons and CDt dopamine signal “stable reward value” in contrast to “flexible reward value” in other striatal areas. However, the lack of reward responses in CDt dopamine is inconsistent with pure value signaling. Rather, CDt and clSNc dopamine neurons are activated by valued visual stimuli specifically, and CDt plays a role in saccades toward such stimuli.

## Roles for TS in Auditory Discrimination

The role of TS in tone-guided behavior is well-characterized in rodents (Figure 2B). Similar to visual stimulus selectivity in CDt neurons, TS activity encodes sound identity tonotopically [25–27]. Furthermore, when distinct tones were paired with reward at a left or right port, TS-projecting auditory cortex inputs responsive to the tone associated with contralateral reward were selectively potentiated [26]. TS activity during the tone encoded little information about upcoming choice [25] (but see [28]), and did not change when tone-port associations were reversed [25], suggesting that TS activity during tone, like visual-stimulus responses in monkeys, encodes sensory features rather than the next action. Accordingly, optogenetic activation of TS did not induce movement by itself, in contrast to optogenetic activation of DLS which caused contralateral turns [25,29]. However, when paired with a tone, optogenetic activation of either TS-projecting auditory cortical inputs or TS neurons biased port selection [25,28,30]. Supporting a role for TS in auditory-guided decisions, pharmacological or chemogenetic inhibition of either TS or projections to TS from auditory cortex or auditory thalamus significantly impaired performance [25,31]. Moreover, optogenetic inhibition of dopamine inputs to TS during tone presentation acutely impaired choice [32]. Taken together, these results suggest that TS and TS dopamine activity is important for either tone discrimination or tone-guided action selection, with further research needed to disambiguate these two possibilities.

## Roles for TS in avoidance of a threatening stimulus

Another line of work has demonstrated that TS-projecting dopamine neurons encode threatening stimuli. TS dopamine neurons are generally excited by physically salient (also conceivable as threatening) external stimuli such as tone, odor, air puff and aggressive conspecifics, but are not reliably excited by reward [33–35]. Moreover, they are not excited by other negative events such as reward omission and bitter water, so they are unlikely to signal negative value or motivational value [34].

Ablation and optogenetic experiments have confirmed the importance of TS-projecting dopamine neurons in threat response. Ablation of these neurons impairs choice between two water ports with distinct outcomes: while control mice avoided a port that delivered water with an air puff, preferring a port dispensing only water, ablation mice did not avoid the same (Figure 2C); yet both groups were able to learn to avoid a port dispensing less water or water with a bitter taste [34]. Thus TS-projecting dopamine neurons facilitate avoidance of threatening stimuli but appear dispensable for reward value-based choice. Optogenetic experiments support this finding: during fear conditioning, optogenetic inhibition of TS-projecting dopamine neurons during a shock-predicting tone (or inhibiting TS D1-MSNs at tone or shock) impaired subsequent fear recall, measured by tone-induced freezing [29,36] (Figure 2D). Fear conditioning itself increased TS responses to the shock-predicting tone, an increase dependent on TS dopamine [36]. Finally, TS activation acutely increased freezing [37], suggesting that TS impacts action selection following a threat in addition to fear learning.

Further supporting a role for TS in threat-mediated behavior, TS-projecting dopamine neurons were strongly excited by a novel stimulus, and their responses persisted only if the stimulus was associated with a threat such as air puff [33,34] or electric shock [36,38]. In a more naturalistic setting, TS dopamine neurons were implicated in determining novel object avoidance [34,39,40] (Figure 2E). TS dopamine neurons were activated at the moment mice were closest to a novel object in each approach bout [34,39], and the magnitude of this response predicted individual variability in novel object exploration: while mice with intrinsically stronger TS dopamine activation tended to be more avoidant, those with ablation of TS-projecting dopamine neurons tended to be bolder [34,39]. These studies suggest that TS dopamine response to novel stimuli may determine whether the animal proceeds to future avoidance of novelty, potentially by setting stimulus-associated threat predictions. Interestingly, CDt neurons in monkeys also show robust responses to novel objects [21,41], although minimal data exists regarding responses of CDt-projecting dopamine neurons to novelty (but see [42]).

## Roles for TS in attentional shift and sensory representation

These varied roles of TS may appear incongruous: depending on the context, TS and TS dopamine are responsible for object-directed saccades, tone-guided choice, or threat avoidance (Figure 2). One possibility is that distinct subregions of TS, or different subpopulations of TS neurons and TS-projecting dopamine neurons, mediate each function. Alternatively, these apparently disparate roles may each be expressions of a common circuit function. We propose one such common framework, inspired by evolutionary perspectives [43–45]: TS promotes a quick (potentially sub-second) attentional shift (e.g., a saccade or covert monitoring) toward salient sensory information, facilitating subsequent behavioral responses such as sustained orientation or avoidance, depending on the nature of the stimulus (Figure 3). Notably, cdlSNr, directly downstream of CDt, is activated by both rewarding and threatening stimuli [42], and monkeys preferentially saccade towards novel or threatening objects as well as rewarding ones [46]. Thus, initial saccade preference, and tightly linked CDt activity, may be a readout for stimulus salience. The appearance of salient stimuli may first trigger CDt activity leading to saccades as an initial alerting response to stimulus salience, followed by further behavioral responses as needed, such as sustained orientation (tracking, pursuit) or avoidance.

Indeed, the anatomical position of TS suggests its alerting signal is well-poised to drive both orienting and avoidance behavior. One of the major projection targets of the TS-SNL pathway is the SC (Figure 1, Figure 3), an evolutionarily conserved region which mediates orienting and avoidance through distinct outputs. In the lamprey, for example, moderately salient (slow-looming) stimuli activate SC projections to the contralateral brainstem (“crossed” pathway) to produce stimulus-directed orienting, while highly salient (fast-looming) stimuli activate SC outputs to both contralateral and ipsilateral brainstem (“uncrossed pathway”), leading to less directed, evasive behavior [47]. In mice, optogenetic stimulation of the crossed pathway elicits quick contralateral orienting followed by contralateral turning, while optogenetic stimulation of the uncrossed pathway elicits quick upwards head movements, followed by defensive behaviors such as retreat and flight [48]. Across species, TS and TS dopamine activation likely influence the SC pathways engaged by salient stimuli and resulting behavior. Importantly, TS activity and behavioral response to the same stimuli may differ between species, with a stimulus’ physical salience/threat level determined by species-specific combinations of factors (e.g. stimulus location, movement and size) [43,47,49]. Through this framework, we can consider reward-associated stimuli in the object-saccade task as being moderately salient to monkeys, and thus engaging only the “crossed” pathway to trigger stimulus-directed orienting. Highly physically salient stimuli such as electric shock, air puff, looming stimuli and threat-predicting stimuli, on the other hand, may strongly engage the SC avoidance (“uncrossed”) pathway, which projects to IC, PAG and CnF (Figure 3), regions key for evasive responses [18,50]. Interestingly, SNL projects to IC, PAG, and CnF directly as well as indirectly (through SC), suggesting multiple routes to induce avoidance [18]. Moreover, SNL preferentially projects to medial and central SC, which monitor the upper visual field to mediate avoidance of airborne predators, but not to lateral SC, which monitors the ground for food [18,43]. Based on the close anatomical relationship between TS and brain areas involved in avoidance, and established roles for the SC in both orienting and avoidance, we propose that TS is specialized to promote a stimulus-guided attentional shift that facilitates subsequent orienting and/or avoidance behavior. Whether TS activity directly informs the decision to orient and/or avoid depending on salience level (our proposed model), or simply acts as a permissive signal for a decision formed elsewhere, requires further investigation.

The idea that TS circuitry facilitates orienting to moderately salient stimuli such as reward-predicting stimuli also accounts for the role of TS in tone-guided choice tasks. After extensive training, such tasks, which unnaturally pair a salient stimulus (tone) with a reward-associated location (port), may exploit an ancient TS circuit for orientation towards a stimulus: TS may drive attention towards the tone and facilitate subsequent orienting to the paired port (Figure 3). Because each TS neuron has both spatial and stimulus selectivity, TS neurons could gradually learn linked combinations of these features during intensive training, allowing TS to facilitate both attention to the tone and subsequent orientation towards an associated port. Alternatively, TS might be engaged not for turning itself, but for initial direction of attention towards the auditory stimulus, akin to the function of a saccade towards visual stimuli. This latter possibility, however, may be less consistent with findings that stimulation of TS neurons during tones induces a contralateral port bias [25,30,51].

Importantly, in parallel with its outputs to the brainstem for behavioral control, TS may also influence behavior by affecting sensory representation (Figure 3). A classical study mapping the structure of cortico-basal ganglia-thalamo-cortical loops found that CDt forms a loop structure back to TeA [6], suggesting a potential influence on object recognition. Furthermore, a recent study indicated that in perceptually-demanding tone discrimination tasks, TS regulates tone representation in the medial geniculate nucleus (MGN, ‘auditory thalamus’) via a cvGP-cTRN pathway [52,53] (Figure 1). Thus, manipulation of CDt/TS or TS dopamine in experimental settings may distort sensory representation and perception, which may cause a deficit in sensory discrimination itself, rather than or in addition to a deficit in action selection. Whether the same TS neurons regulate switches in attention and sensory representation remains to be seen.

## Roles for dopamine in TS: Reinforcement and modulation of attention

If the role of TS is to facilitate stimulus-guided action, be it orienting or avoidance, what is the role of dopamine in TS? Given its demonstrated role in fear learning [36,38], a strong possibility is that TS dopamine functions in a threatening context as a teaching signal, similar to the demonstrated role for dopamine in reward-based reinforcement learning [54] (Figure 4A). In this spirit, Akiti et al. proposed a simple threat-based reinforcement-learning model to account for the finding that TS dopamine underlies novelty avoidance, with TS dopamine signaling “threat prediction error”, instead of reward prediction error (RPE) classically proposed for dopamine [39]. Because it could be catastrophic for an animal to rely on actual experiences of harm to learn to predict potential threat, this model proposes that an animal may first use physical salience – e.g., stimulus size, intensity and movement – as an initial estimate of threat prediction (‘shaping bonus’) [55] (Figure 4B). This is consistent with the finding that TS dopamine activity is modulated by the intensity of novel stimuli from multiple modalities [5]. The initial estimate is later refined by experiences of salient events involving the object, and eventually converges to a more accurate prediction of net future salience associated with the stimulus [39]. In this sense, the dopamine teaching signal in TS can be interpreted as a more generalized ‘salience prediction error’, which may be used to train TS to predict future salience. Once the salience predicted by TS exceeds a predetermined avoidance threshold, animals may avoid the associated stimulus. Using this model to simulate threat prediction learning with dopamine in TS, the authors could account for complex temporal dynamics and individual variability in naturalistic interactions with a novel object. In short, TS dopamine may link primitive sensory features (physical salience) with behavioral avoidance. This idea is supported by a recent study, which found that TS dopamine release, the physical salience of a threatening stimulus, and stimulus avoidance rate are all correlated, and manipulation of TS dopamine bidirectionally modulated the link between physical salience and avoidance (Figure 4C) [15].

Compared to their well-defined role in avoidance, the precise role of CDt/TS dopamine in mediating object-reward or tone-port associations is controversial. For example, in auditory discrimination tasks, one study observed induction of a contralateral bias upon unilateral activation of dopamine axons [51], whereas another study observed no bias even with unilateral stimulation, leading the authors to pool unilateral and bilateral stimulation [56]. The discrepancy between these studies remains to be resolved in future work. In either case, the salience prediction error proposed to facilitate threat avoidance may be also used to learn orienting towards salient stimuli in a non-threatening environment. Through the lens of our proposed model (Figure 3), perturbations disrupting TS dopamine (thus altering salience prediction error) or TS neuron activity (thus altering the net future salience prediction) could impact initial attention to the guiding tone, subsequent port-orienting behavior, and/or resultant learning across the session.

Importantly, dopamine release in TS during cue presentation has also been shown to influence on-going choice behavior [32] and/or learning [36]. A recent study likewise found that ablation of TS-projecting dopamine neurons affects avoidance behavior from the very first trial, suggesting acute effects of TS dopamine in addition to effects on learning across trials [15]. These studies suggest that TS dopamine may acutely enhance TS signaling, influencing sensory representation and/or attentional control over a downstream orienting/avoidance pathway that results in both a bias in immediate choice in the current trial, and enhanced learning.

## Conclusion

The TS has been implicated in diverse domains, including visual orientation, tone-guided choice, and avoidance of threatening stimuli. We propose a general framework for understanding these varied functions, placing TS at the center of a circuit linking salient sensory stimuli to conserved action programs. Specifically, we propose that TS learns a prediction of future physical salience associated with stimuli and provides this information to ancient circuitry responsible for rapid control of attention to drive responsive action, especially orientation (upon moderate physical salience prediction) and/or avoidance (upon high physical salience prediction). We propose that TS dopamine functions as a teaching signal to facilitate this prediction. Future work is called for to understand how the proposed role of TS in attentional shift is implemented across varied contexts, whether distinct cell types or subareas within TS are differentially engaged depending on the task at hand, and how acute and learning effects of TS and TS dopamine activity are combined with information from other striatal subregions to facilitate balanced decision-making.

## Abstract

Type A aortic dissection (TAAD) with malperfusion carries high mortality and morbidity despite current surgical techniques; new approaches are needed to improve outcomes. This study evaluates the outcomes of patients undergoing intraoperative assessment and treatment of distal malperfusion during central aortic repair.

A retrospective review of 551 TAAD patients from 2000 to 2023 identified 54 patients with clinical malperfusion of the mesenteric, renal, spinal cord or iliofemoral based on clinical presentation, imaging and biomarkers. Patients with radiological aortic branch involvement but without clinical symptoms were excluded. Patients were grouped into: standard approach (n = 36), where central aortic repair was followed by postoperative ICU care, and comprehensive approach (n = 18), where intraoperative evaluation for persistent malperfusion was conducted after termination of cardiopulmonary bypass, with immediate intervention if needed. The primary outcome was operative mortality. Secondary outcomes included resolution of malperfusion.

Of 54 patients, 41% (n = 22) had mesenteric, 46% (n = 25) renal, 11% (n = 6) spinal and 76% (n = 41) iliofemoral malperfusion. The comprehensive approach was significantly associated with reduced odds of the composite outcome [odds ratio (OR): 0.17, 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.04–0.63, P = 0.008] and increased odds of resolving malperfusion (OR: 4.55, 95% CI: 1.26–16.44, P = 0.021). In the mesenteric subgroup (n = 22), odds of malperfusion resolution were markedly higher (OR: 19.30, 95% CI: 2.17–171.65, P = 0.008). However, no significant associations were found in the limb (OR: 3.17, P = 0.107) or renal subgroups (OR: 4.38, P = 0.164).

Patients with TAAD undergoing immediate intraoperative evaluation to identify and treat distal malperfusion simultaneously with central aortic repair may benefit from lower rates of complications and bowel resection. Further studies with larger datasets are needed to validate this approach.

## Abstract

## INTRODUCTION

Patients with type A aortic dissection (TAAD) and distal malperfusion represent a high-risk group with significant morbidity and mortality, highlighting the urgent need for refined management strategies [1]. The decision-making process involved in the management of distal end-organ malperfusion is often complex and continues to be a subject of debate [2]. While the general consensus is to proceed with prompt ascending aortic replacement, which effectively resolves distal malperfusion in the majority of patients [3–5], alternative strategies have been proposed. Some approaches advocate for the prioritization of treating malperfusion before addressing aortic repair. However, this strategy poses risks such as interval aortic rupture and may not be feasible in certain situations, such as when cardiac tamponade is present [1, 5]. This debate underscores the complexity of managing high-risk cases and the need for a comprehensive evaluation of different treatment approaches. In this study, we explore a novel strategy by examining outcomes in patients who undergo simultaneous detection and treatment of malperfusion during central aortic repair. We hypothesize that this comprehensive approach will result in more favourable outcomes compared to the standard approach of central aortic repair alone.

## PATIENTS AND METHODS

### Ethical statement

This study was conducted in accordance with the principles outlined in the WMA Declaration of Helsinki and WMA Declaration of Taipei regarding the ethical collection, storage and use of data. Written informed consent for the use of intraoperative images was obtained. Approval for the study was obtained from the Massachusetts General Hospital Institutional Review Board (2024P000688, 1999P009949), and informed consent was waived due to the retrospective nature of the study.

### Patient selection

A retrospective review of the institutional database was conducted to identify patients with TAAD who presented to Massachusetts General Hospital between 2000 and 2023 with clinical signs and symptoms of mesenteric, renal, spinal or limb malperfusion.

Inclusion criteria were adult patients aged 18 years or older with confirmed TAAD and clinical signs of distal malperfusion. Exclusion criteria included patients who had radiological evidence of involvement of an aortic branch but did not exhibit clinical symptoms, as well as patients who initially underwent an endovascular approach followed by central aortic repair, those with isolated coronary or cerebral malperfusion, and those who underwent non-operative management for their dissection.

Diagnosis of distal malperfusion was based on the presence of symptoms and signs indicative of disturbed blood flow to specific end-organ systems. Distal malperfusion syndromes included: limb malperfusion, identified by loss of pulses, clinical signs of limb ischaemia or elevated creatinine kinase levels; mesenteric malperfusion, indicated by abdominal tenderness, lactate acidosis and transaminitis; and renal malperfusion, defined as acute renal failure or acute-on-chronic renal failure associated with compromise of the renal arterial branch [2, 6–10]. Data on these clinical presentations as well as radiological involvement were collected from the hospital aortic dissection database and confirmed by review of electronic medical records. Confirmation of malperfusion syndrome required radiographic documentation that dissection involved the relevant aortic branch vessels, or documentation indicating the presence of clinical malperfusion in the surgeon’s operative or clinical notes.

### Surgical approach

Patients were separated into two cohorts based on intraoperative details. All patients underwent immediate central aortic repair, with the extent of aortic resection up to the surgeon’s discretion. In the standard group, patients were transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU) at the end of surgical repair, without any additional investigational or interventional procedures to identify or treat residual distal malperfusion. In the comprehensive surgery group, patients underwent additional intraoperative evaluation for persistent malperfusion concurrently with their aortic repair post-cardiopulmonary bypass, using intravascular ultrasound (IVUS), angiography, or both in addition to other methods such as femoral artery evaluation to assess for persistent malperfusion. Any persistent malperfusion that was identified was addressed immediately, before leaving the operating room. Operations are ideally performed in a hybrid operating room with fixed imaging capabilities. If unavailable, a fluoroscopy-compatible operating room is used, with a portable imaging system available as needed. Upon arrival, the patient is jointly assessed by the cardiac and vascular surgery teams for immediate central aortic repair. Following completion of the central aortic repair, which can involve any proximal or aortic arch operation, the distal aorta is evaluated using a combination of transoesophageal echocardiography (TEE), IVUS or invasive angiography to confirm resolution of malperfusion in the distal vascular beds. This assessment can be performed either via a transfemoral approach or, alternatively, in an antegrade fashion by accessing the ascending aortic graft in the chest, which provides easy access to the true lumen of the aorta (Fig. 2).

### Outcome measures

The primary outcome was operative mortality, defined as in-hospital or 30-day mortality. Pre-specified and clinically relevant composite outcomes were used to enhance the power to detect differences between groups [11]. Secondary outcomes included malperfusion-related reoperation, complications and resolved malperfusion. Malperfusion-related reoperation was defined as a return to the operating room or endovascular suite for any of the following malperfusion-related reinterventions: stenting, fasciotomy, exploratory laparotomy or lower limb revascularization. Composite outcome of death, reoperation or acute renal failure requiring hemodialysis was measured. Resolution of malperfusion was defined overall as the absence of complications related to malperfusion post-operatively, and individually based on previous literature [12], as follows: resolved mesenteric malperfusion was indicated by decreasing lactic and pancreatic enzyme levels, reduced acidosis, relief of abdominal pain or feeding difficulties, and absence of the need for exploratory laparotomy or bowel resection during hospital stay; resolved renal malperfusion was indicated by decreasing creatinine levels or maintained urine output without need for renal replacement therapy; and resolved limb malperfusion was indicated by resolution of ischaemic symptoms, return of blood flow or pulse, and no development of compartment syndrome requiring fasciotomy. Resolved malperfusion was calculated as the proportion of patients without malperfusion-related complications among those with the specific malperfusion.

### Statistical methods

Categorical variables were presented as count (n) and percentage (%). Continuous variables were reported as median ± interquartile range (IQR) or mean ± standard deviation (SD). Comparisons between groups were performed using the chi-square (χ2) or Fisher’s exact test when the expected frequency of any cell was <5 for categorical variables, and Student’s t-test for continuous variables. Two-sided P-values were used, with statistical significance determined at a threshold of 0.05. To address potential confounding in the observational design, inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was employed based on a propensity score model. The propensity score was estimated using a multivariable logistic regression model, with surgical approach as the dependent variable and age, gender, presence or absence of comorbidities, severity of clinical symptoms of malperfusion at presentation, where patients presenting with compartment syndrome necessitating fasciotomy or severe abdominal pain prompting the surgeons to perform an exploratory laparotomy was adjusted for, and year that the surgery was performed divided into three periods (2000–9, 2010–19, 2020–23) as independent variables. Covariate selection was based on clinical judgement. IPTW was calculated as the inverse of the propensity score for treated patients and the inverse of 1 minus the propensity score for untreated patients.

Unstabilized weights were used to minimize bias while preserving interpretability. Balance between groups after weighting was assessed using standardized mean differences (SMDs), with an SMD < 0.1 considered indicative of adequate balance [13]. For weighted analyses, the primary outcome was compared using logistic regression, accounting for the IPTW. Secondary outcomes were analysed similarly. Robust standard errors were calculated to account for the weighted nature of the data. Sensitivity analyses were conducted to assess extreme weights and evaluate potential violations of positivity. A priori subgroup analysis stratified by anatomic site of malperfusion was performed. Era analysis was conducted by dividing the study period into two timeframes: pre-2015 and post-2015. This classification was based on the increased adoption of comprehensive surgery at our institution after 2015. All analyses were conducted using Stata (version 18.0, StataCorp LLC, College Station, TX, USA).

## RESULTS

Among 551 patients with DeBakey type I, we identified 137 patients with probable malperfusion, including both clinical and radiological malperfusion. After electronic health records review, we confirmed a total of 54 patients with clinical distal malperfusion (Fig. 1). Of those, 29 (54%) patients had more than one anatomic site of distal malperfusion. Overall, 22 (41%) patients had mesenteric, 25 (46%) renal, 41 (76%) limb and 6 (11%) spinal malperfusion. Baseline characteristics were largely similar between groups (Table 1). There were no significant differences between the groups regarding the types of operative procedures performed for central aortic repair (Table 2). ## DISCUSSION

Despite advances in treatment of acute aortic dissection, mortality for patients with malperfusion remains high [14]. Previous discussions have debated whether to prioritize immediate aortic repair and primary entry-tear resection to restore perfusion to affected organs, particularly in cases of limb malperfusion [7, 15–17], or to address malperfusion before central aortic repair, especially in cases of mesenteric malperfusion [7, 18–21]. Debate also continues regarding the optimal extent of aortic arch replacement for patients with acute TAAD, but most of the discussion has focused on the effects of extended aortic replacement on aortic remodelling and late aortic reoperations, with only few studies focusing on patients with malperfusion [22]. This paper evaluates whether patients who receive immediate assessment and treatment for malperfusion during central aortic repair experience better outcomes compared to those who undergo central aortic repair alone with postoperative monitoring and treatment for malperfusion. To our knowledge, this is the first study to examine the outcomes of a new approach whereby patients with distal malperfusion undergo central aortic repair with concurrent assessment for ongoing malperfusion during the index operation. In this study, we observed no statistically significant difference in operative mortality between the comprehensive and standard groups, despite a clinical trend in favour of the comprehensive group, likely due to the sample size being insufficiently powered to detect variations in operative mortality alone. Patients who received immediate assessment and management of malperfusion during central aortic repair generally experienced a clinical trend towards fewer malperfusion-related complications such as bowel resection and fasciotomy. There was zero incidence of bowel resection in the comprehensive group vs 17% in the standard group (46% when only considering patients who presented with mesenteric malperfusion), despite more patients presenting with abdominal pain in the comprehensive group.

At our institution, TAAD patients are jointly evaluated by the cardiac and vascular surgery teams upon arrival. In patients with clinical or severe radiologic malperfusion on preoperative evaluation, IVUS, angiography, or often both are performed at the conclusion of cardiopulmonary bypass to evaluate the blood flow in the distal branch vessels. Angioplasty, stenting or other revascularization procedures (e.g. bypass) are performed if there is imaging evidence of ongoing compromise of blood flow to the end organs. Exploratory laparotomy may be performed to evaluate bowel viability based on clinical judgement. In our experience, extended aortic arch replacement, even with a frozen elephant trunk, does not guarantee resolution of distal malperfusion and further interventions may be necessary to restore perfusion. We feel that it is a paradox in clinical practice that while most surgeons will not leave the operating room if there is a pulse deficit in the extremities at the conclusion of the aortic repair without performing additional revascularization procedures to restore flow to the extremity, but in patients with mesenteric malperfusion, which has the highest likelihood of worse outcomes, are often content to ‘go to the ICU and follow’. With our approach we were able to decrease the incidence of postoperative bowel resection in patients in the comprehensive group. Other groups have also shown the advantages of using a hybrid approach to treat acute TAAD. Dalal et al. [8] compared outcomes of 125 matched TAAD patients with malperfusion treated in a hybrid operating room with angiography and intervention alongside central aortic repair, to those treated in traditional operating room using historical controls. Treatment of patients in the hybrid operating room was associated with improved survival and increased the likelihood of patients undergoing angiography or intervention. In their study patients with or without malperfusion were included, while in our study, we restricted the sample to patients presenting with clinical distal malperfusion, using concomitant controls. Interestingly, Dalal et al. observed a clinical trend towards more bowel resections and exploratory laparotomies in the hybrid operating room group, primarily due to bowel ischaemia. In contrast, in our comprehensive management group, none of the patients experienced bowel ischaemia requiring resection.

Several limitations of our study must be acknowledged. Foremost, we recognize that the sample size may be insufficiently powered to detect significant differences in operative mortality. However, using Pearson’s chi-square test at a significance level of 0.05 and a desired power of 80%, a difference of 5% (0.2 vs 0.15) in operative mortality would require a total sample size of 1812 patients, 906 patients per group. Given the rarity of the condition and the surgical approach, achieving this sample size is not feasible. Although we employed composite outcomes to mitigate this limitation, the inherent constraints of a retrospective analysis may still impact the precision of our findings. The propensity score model used to adjust for confounding may be prone to model misspecification due to the small sample size. Despite efforts to mitigate this by selecting relevant covariates based on subject matter expertise, residual confounding cannot be ruled out. Additionally, a limitation of our study is the retrospective assessment of clinical malperfusion, particularly with older health records. Inconsistent documentation of branch involvement and the distinction between static and dynamic malperfusion may have affected the comprehensiveness of our findings. Moreover, the observational nature of the study limits the ability to establish causality, and reliance on data from a single institution may restrict the external validity of the results.

Despite these notable limitations, our current findings suggest that patients with mesenteric malperfusion in the comprehensive surgery group, despite being more severely ill, exhibit a higher proportion of resolved mesenteric malperfusion and did not require bowel resection following exploratory laparotomies. This observation underscores the need for further investigation into the utility of IVUS or angiography in this context. Future studies with larger sample sizes and prospective designs are needed to validate this approach.
